q-339260.name: Question 1
q-339260.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,(\pi /6)^{+}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-339260.html:
Question 1

Evaluate the following limit:
limx→(π/6)+sin⁡(4x−π3)=
√32​
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Substituting x=π6 directly into the limit, we have limx→(π/6)+sin⁡(4x−π3)=sin⁡(4⋅π6−π3)=sin⁡(2π3−π3)=sin⁡(π3)=32.

q-339283.name: Question 2
q-339283.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /{3}^{+}}({cos}^{2}⁡(x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) & ={cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \\  & =\frac{1+\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-339283.html:
Question 2
?
Evaluate the following limit:
limx→π/3+(cos2⁡(x)+cos⁡(x)sin⁡(x))=
1+√34​
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Substituting x=π3 directly into the limit, we have

limx→π/3+(cos2⁡(x)+cos⁡(x)sin⁡(x))=cos2⁡(π3)+cos⁡(π3)⋅sin⁡(π3)=(12)2+12⋅32=14+34=1+34.
q-339283.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit of Sine or Cosine

q-47045.name: Question 3
q-47045.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14258704/assets/7955bebdbd0ba4e92f8f56ed8a2ddb6cec57315b20c906b9735f82d1d9e19f0b.png)

As $x$ increases, the graph oscillates between the values $y=-1$ and $y=1$ indefinitely. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{2}x)=DNE.
$$
